metadata.title: AI Glossary
metadata.note: Terms follow the Stanford HAI glossary. Definitions are short paraphrases written for this file, not copied text. See the source page for the original wording.

terms.definition: An attack in which someone covertly interferes with the process of training or distilling a model so that the resulting model behaves in the attacker's favor.
A hypothetical AI system able to learn, reason, and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks at or beyond human level.
AI systems that act with some autonomy: they interpret goals, plan steps, use tools such as browsers, code, or APIs, learn from feedback, and carry tasks through to completion.
The effort to make an AI system's goals and behavior match human values, rules, and intentions.
Standardized tests used to measure and compare AI systems on tasks such as question answering, image recognition, coding, or instruction following.
The ability to work with AI productively and responsibly, which includes knowing what it can and cannot do, judging its outputs critically, using it ethically, and keeping pace as it changes.
The field concerned with making AI systems reliable and free from harmful behavior, including when they are powerful, widely used, or in unfamiliar situations.
The combined software, hardware, and computing resources that support every stage of the AI lifecycle.
The end-to-end process of building, deploying, and maintaining an AI system, from data preparation through training, testing, and deployment.
A set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, much like a recipe.
A situation where many organizations rely on the same or very similar algorithms, models, or training data, so errors and biases are shared widely.
A network of AI systems or agents that share information and coordinate their actions as a collective.
The science and engineering of building intelligent machines. The term was coined in 1955 by John McCarthy, Stanford's first AI faculty member.
A technique in neural networks that lets a model concentrate on the most relevant parts of its input when producing an output.
Technology, including AI, carrying out tasks according to explicit instructions and parameters that a human has defined in advance.
The method by which neural networks learn from errors, by working backward through the layers to find which parts contributed to the mistake.
Graphical models that use probabilities to show how variables influence one another, similar to a map of cause and effect.
When an AI system produces outcomes that systematically favor or disadvantage certain groups of people.
Datasets so large that conventional data-processing tools cannot handle them, often analyzed with AI to uncover patterns and trends.
A program that simulates conversation with people through text or voice.
Software, also called proprietary, whose code is kept private and cannot be freely viewed, modified, or used by the public.
A field of AI that lets computers detect, identify, and interpret visual information from images and video.
The amount of input, such as text, that an AI model can take in and work with at one time.
A learning technique in which a model compares similar and dissimilar examples to figure out what makes items alike or different.
Expanding a training dataset by creating altered versions of existing data rather than collecting new data.
Finding patterns and trends in large datasets using statistics and machine learning.
An attack in which someone deliberately inserts, changes, or mislabels data in a model's training set to corrupt what the model learns.
An algorithm that predicts outcomes by asking a series of yes/no questions that split the data until it reaches a conclusion.
A branch of machine learning that uses large, multi-layer neural networks to learn complex patterns from data automatically.
Generative models that create content such as images by learning to add noise to data and then remove it.
Simplifying complex data by cutting the number of variables while keeping the most important information.
Numerical vectors that represent words, images, or other objects in a way that captures their meaning or characteristics.
Techniques that combine several models, often individually weak, to produce a prediction more accurate and robust than any single one.
Designing, building, and deploying AI in line with human values, fairness, transparency, and societal well-being.
AI programs that imitate the decisions of human experts in a narrow domain using a knowledge base and mostly if-then rules.
Methods that make an AI system's decisions understandable to people instead of leaving it an opaque black box.
Training a model across many devices or servers that each hold their own data, so the data never leaves its original location.
Getting a model to handle a new task after seeing only a handful of examples.
Taking a pre-trained model and training it further on data specific to a task or domain.
Large models, often transformers, trained on broad and varied data so they can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
A highly capable, general-purpose AI model at or near the cutting edge of current development.
AI systems that create new content such as text, images, music, code, or video.
An architecture of two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, that compete with each other to produce realistic synthetic data.
A family of large language models built on the transformer architecture that generate human-like text from prompts.
A chip originally built for rendering graphics that performs many calculations in parallel, which makes it well suited to training AI models.
Cases where an AI system produces false, misleading, or invented information and presents it as fact.
An approach to AI that puts human needs, values, and well-being first throughout development and deployment.
The study and practice of how people use and engage with computer systems.
A design in which people provide feedback or step in as part of an AI system's operation.
A setting for a machine learning model that is chosen before training begins rather than learned from data.
A large technology company running vast data-center networks that can quickly scale computing, storage, and cloud services to meet demand.
When a trained model makes predictions or decisions on new data it has not seen before.
How well humans can understand the way an AI system reaches its decisions or predictions.
A simple algorithm for classification and regression that decides based on the closest examples in the data.
A structured database that represents information as a network of entities and the relationships between them.
An AI system trained on huge amounts of text so it can understand and generate human-like language.
A compressed, abstract space into which complex data such as images, text, or audio is encoded, capturing its essential features and patterns.
The practice of managing the full lifecycle of LLM-based applications running in production.
A mathematical measure of how far a model's predictions are from the correct values. Also called a cost function or objective function.
A branch of AI in which computers learn patterns and make decisions from data instead of following explicitly programmed rules.
A mathematical model of a sequence of events in which the probability of the next event depends only on the current state, not on how it was reached.
Practices that blend machine learning, software engineering, and DevOps to deploy, monitor, and maintain ML models reliably in production.
A simplified mathematical or computational representation of a real-world system or relationship, used to make predictions or understand patterns.
A decline in a model's performance over time because real-world data has shifted away from what it was trained on.
AI that can process, understand, and generate several kinds of data, such as text, images, audio, and video.
A branch of AI that enables computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
A computational model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of connected artificial neurons that process and pass along information.
A method that improves a model by adjusting its settings so that it makes fewer mistakes.
When a model memorizes its training data too closely, including errors and random quirks, and so performs poorly on new data.
An AI model whose weights, code, training data (or a detailed auditable account of it), and tools are all available to download, run, inspect, reproduce, modify, and improve.
An AI model whose core components, chiefly its weights, are publicly released so anyone can download it.
Software whose underlying design is freely available for anyone to view and use.
An internal variable in a machine learning model that is learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistics, and machine learning to forecast future outcomes or trends.
Crafting instructions, or prompts, carefully so that a language model produces the desired output.
A security attack that uses malicious input to trick a large language model into behaving in unintended ways.
A technique that improves a language model's answers by letting it look up external, current information before responding.
An AI system built to solve complex problems by working through a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
A type of machine learning in which an agent improves through trial and error by acting within an environment.
The frameworks, principles, and practices that guide ethical and safe development and use of AI.
The field combining engineering and computer science, increasingly with AI, to design and build machines that perform physical tasks.
The ability to understand and reason about the three-dimensional world, including how objects relate, move, and interact in space.
A training approach in which a model creates its own learning tasks from raw data and learns by solving them.
Working out the meaning of language by examining relationships among words, phrases, and symbols.
Predictable mathematical relationships showing how model performance improves as model size, training data, and compute grow.
A machine learning approach in which models learn from labeled data, meaning inputs paired with the correct outputs.
Artificially generated data produced by algorithms or simulations rather than gathered from real-world events.
A container for numbers arranged in multiple dimensions, like a more general version of a spreadsheet.
Splitting text into smaller units, called tokens, such as words, word parts, or characters, that language models can process.
Earlier approaches to AI that relied on hand-written rules, logic, and human-defined knowledge instead of learning from data.
The collection of examples, such as text, images, or audio, used to teach a machine learning model a task.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task.
A neural network architecture that uses attention to relate all parts of the input to one another at once rather than one step at a time.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 of whether a machine can behave so intelligently that it is indistinguishable from a human.
A machine learning approach in which models find patterns and structure in data that has no labels or predefined categories.
A database designed to store and quickly search high-dimensional vectors that represent data such as text, images, or audio.
An adaptation of the transformer architecture, originally made for language, to analyze images.
The numerical parameters in a neural network that set the strength of connections between neurons and shape how the model processes information.
A model's ability to perform tasks or recognize categories it was never explicitly trained on, using its general knowledge.
